topic: The Trap of Patterns: Moser's Circle Problem
target_audience: High school students and math enthusiasts

sections.title: The Hook: A Game of Slicing
lecture_lines: Imagine placing points along a circle's edge.
Connect every point to every other point with lines.
How many regions can we divide this circle into?
animations: Draw a white circle (#FFFFFF) at the center of the grid. Place two distinct yellow points (#FFFF00) at non-uniform angles on the circumference (B059).
Draw a yellow chord (#FFFF00) between the two points. The two resulting regions of the circle briefly glow with a light blue fill (#ADD8E6).
Add a third yellow point (#FFFF00) at a non-uniform angle. Draw chords to all other points. The four resulting regions glow with light blue fill (#ADD8E6).
Add a fourth yellow point (#FFFF00) and connect it to all previous points. Highlight the 8 resulting regions.
Display the rule text in the lecture area: 'Connect every point to every other point.' (B021)

sections.title: Establishing the 'Obvious' Pattern
lecture_lines: With one point, we have just one region.
Two points create a chord and two regions.
Three points divide the circle into four distinct areas.
Four points yield eight regions, and five yield sixteen.
The pattern seems clear: the regions double every time.
animations: Show a table on the right side of the screen (columns 3-6) with headers 'n (points)' and 'R (regions)'. Add the row: n=1, R=1.
Update the table to show n=2, R=2 and n=3, R=4. Corresponding circle diagrams appear briefly above the table.
Update the table to show n=4, R=8 and n=5, R=16.
Draw a blue box (#0000FF) around the R values (1, 2, 4, 8, 16).
Display the predicted formula in the lecture area (B021): 'R = 2^(n-1)?' in blue (#0000FF).

sections.title: The Twist: Breaking the Pattern
lecture_lines: Surely, six points will result in thirty-two regions?
Let's add the sixth point and count carefully.
We count the outer regions and then the inner ones.
Surprisingly, the total count is only thirty-one regions!
Our beautiful doubling pattern has suddenly failed us.
animations: Draw a large white circle (#FFFFFF) with 6 points at non-uniform angles (B059). Connect all 15 chords in yellow (#FFFF00).
A red pointer [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/pointer.svg] moves through the circle, counting regions 1 to 15. Each region pulses green (#00FF00) as it is counted.
The red pointer [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/pointer.svg] continues counting regions 16 to 30. Regions pulse green (#00FF00).
The red pointer [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/pointer.svg] highlights the final 31st region. It pulses bright green (#00FF00).
Display 'R = 31' in large red text (#FF0000) next to the circle. Show '31!= 2^(6-1)' to signify the pattern break.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Euler’s Formula for Planar Graphs
lecture_lines: To solve this, we use Euler's formula for graphs.
In a circle, regions equal edges minus vertices plus one.
This formula calculates regions without manual counting.
animations: Display Euler's Formula: 'V - E + F = 2' in the center, with 'V: Vertices', 'E: Edges', 'F: Faces' labeled in light green (#90EE90).
Show a square [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/square.svg] with one diagonal line. Label the 4 vertices, 5 edges, and 2 internal faces to demonstrate the formula (B042).
Algebraically transform the formula to 'R = E - V + 1' for counting internal regions, and move it to the lecture area (B021).

sections.title: The Mathematical Anatomy
lecture_lines: Vertices include original points and every internal crossing.
Every four points define exactly one unique intersection.
Total internal vertices are calculated as "n choose 4".
Edges are chords plus segments along the circumference.
We use combinations to find all parts of the puzzle.
animations: Highlight 4 points on the circle circumference in magenta (#FF00FF). Show the intersection point of their chords in cyan (#00FFFF).
Display the label 'Internal Vertices = nCr(n, 4)' near the intersection. Repeat for another set of 4 points to show the relationship.
Show a summary: Total V = n + nCr(n, 4) and Total E = 2*nCr(n, 4) + nCr(n, 2) + n in the right visual area (columns 3-6).

sections.title: The Final Formula and Conclusion
lecture_lines: The true formula combines these intersection and chord counts.
It matches the doubling pattern only until five points.
In math, patterns suggest truths, but proofs confirm them.
animations: Combine the terms from the previous step to show the final formula: 'R = nCr(n, 4) + nCr(n, 2) + 1' in a gold box (#FFD700) featuring [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/gold.svg].
Display a comparison table: Column 1 (n=1..6), Column 2 (2^(n-1)), Column 3 (Actual Formula). Highlight the row n=6 where the values diverge (32 vs 31).
Fade out the math and display the closing quote: 'A pattern is a hint, not a law.' in a soft white (#F0F0F0).
